title: Nvidia eyes converting old nuclear plants into AI data centers
content:
Nvidia eyes converting old nuclear plants into massive AI data centers — reusing shut-down German energy sites could reduce the cost and timeline of building from scratch
The plan does not involve using nuclear power.
Nvidia is collaborating with German energy firm PreussenElektra GmbH (PEL) to explore converting old nuclear power plants into AI data centers. In an official announcement on October 21st, the U.S. chipmaker and the German firm entered a preliminary partnership to assess whether the latter's decommissioned nuclear power plant sites in Germany can be converted into high-performance AI data centers. The plan does not involve using nuclear power to power any future data centers. Instead, the project is focused on leveraging the existing power, water, and other infrastructure already present at the sites.
“Our former power plant sites have valuable industrial infrastructure and offer opportunities for new, future-oriented uses. Together with NVIDIA, we intend to conduct a sound assessment of whether and how these conditions can be leveraged for AI factories. In doing so, we are combining the responsible reuse of our sites with new economic opportunities for the regions,” says Guido Knott, Chairman of PEL’s Management Board.
The open-ended exploration will assess existing energy grid links, available land, and industrial infrastructure at the former nuclear sites to see if they meet the strict operational requirements of “AI factories.”
The move aims to find alternatives to building massive data centers from scratch amid the unprecedented AI infrastructure buildout. New data centers require well-located land, industrial-zone approvals, proximity to water infrastructure for cooling, and high-voltage grid connections, things nuclear plants already have. By repurposing these facilities, Nvidia hopes to significantly reduce cost and development timelines.
“AI factories require access to power, land and high-capacity infrastructure, and former industrial sites could provide a strong foundation for this next generation of computing,” said Markus Hacker, senior regional director at Nvidia. Together with PreussenElektra, we will assess how its sites could meet the technical and operational requirements of AI factories and contribute to Germany’s high-performance AI infrastructure.”
Germany permanently shut down its last remaining operational nuclear power plants in April 2023, following the Fukushima nuclear disaster, and is dismantling about 30 nuclear power plants across the country. PreussenElektra is currently responsible for decommissioning and dismantling eight of the plants, which are likely the sites to be assessed. The company, alongside Nvidia, has made it clear that the data center assessment initiative is strictly in an experimental feasibility phase.
No investment amounts, approved development plans, or definitive construction agreements have been finalized yet.

report.summary: Nvidia and PreussenElektra will study whether decommissioned German nuclear plant sites can be reused as AI data centers, without using nuclear power.
report.background: Germany shut down its last operating nuclear reactors in April 2023 after the Fukushima disaster and is dismantling roughly 30 nuclear plants. PreussenElektra is decommissioning eight of them. Meanwhile, the AI boom is driving demand for massive data centers, but new sites face hurdles: suitable land, industrial-zoning approvals, cooling water, and high-voltage grid connections. Decommissioned nuclear sites already have much of that infrastructure. Nvidia is therefore exploring whether these brownfield industrial sites can host AI factories more cheaply and quickly than building from scratch. The partnership is preliminary and focused on feasibility, not on restarting nuclear generation or using nuclear power for the data centers.
key_points: Nvidia and German energy firm PreussenElektra have entered a preliminary partnership to assess whether decommissioned nuclear plant sites can be converted into AI data centers. The project explicitly does not involve using nuclear power; it focuses on reusing existing power, water, land, and industrial infrastructure.

Former nuclear sites offer high-voltage grid links, cooling-water access, large industrial parcels, and existing permits or industrial zoning. Those are exactly the constraints that make new AI data centers slow and expensive to build, so reusing sites could cut both cost and development timelines.

The open-ended feasibility study will examine grid connections, available land, and site infrastructure against the strict operational requirements of Nvidia-style AI factories. No investment amounts, approved development plans, or construction agreements have been finalized.

The plan fits Germany’s post-nuclear transition: about 30 plants are being dismantled, and PreussenElektra is responsible for eight. Reusing sites could create new economic activity for regions losing power-plant jobs, while supporting Germany’s high-performance AI infrastructure ambitions.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the proposal highlights that power, land, water, and grid access—not just chips—are becoming binding constraints on AI expansion. If validated, brownfield AI factories could shorten permitting and construction timelines and make older industrial sites valuable again. For developers, site selection and energy procurement may become as important as GPU supply, and Nvidia could gain influence over where AI capacity is built. For regular users, faster data-center deployment could help meet AI demand, but the effect on prices and service availability will depend on whether these projects move beyond feasibility studies. The plan is not a nuclear revival: it is infrastructure reuse, and no construction or investment has been approved.
report.tools: No specific open-source project or tool was announced. To follow the theme, watch Nvidia’s AI factory reference designs and Omniverse digital-twin planning for site simulation, plus grid-interconnection and cooling-feasibility assessments. PreussenElektra’s site studies are the key official updates. For independent energy-system modeling, open-source tools such as PyPSA can explore grid and load scenarios; OpenMC is used for nuclear analysis but is not part of this partnership.
